Q: Scene References for Unity Chapter Loader SO A:

SceneAsset itself sits in the UnityEditor namespace so you can't reference it in runtime code!

A custom Editor is not a good solution as

  • a) it's pretty overkill since you have to basically reimplement the entire Inspector of the entire component
  • b) it's not reusable if you want to use another scene reference somewhere else

However, I happen to have a solid solution for this - adapted from an existing one and cleaned up (credit links in code).

I use this one quite often in production - unfortunately the script is too large to put it here on SO as a whole

https://github.com/der-hugo/SceneReference/blob/main/SceneReference.cs

In simple words

  • it's based on ISerializationCallbackReceiver
  • in the editor it exposes a SceneAsset field
  • but then it actually stores the scene path to be used on runtime

With this you simply expose

public SceneReference MyScene;

and then can pass it to SceneManager.LoacScene because it implicitly concerts to the according scene path. Additionally it comes with a nice editor in the Inspector with indication whether the scene is correctly added to the build settings - and also buttons to simply do so.

Q: Docker Compose: correct config for MariaDB + MongoDB + Qdrant (ports, env vars, volumes) and how containers should connect? A: 
services:
  db:
    image: mariadb:10.11
    environment:
      MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD: 
      MARIADB_DATABASE: 
    ports:
      - "3306:"
    volumes:
      - ./data/mariadb:/var/lib/mysql

  mongodb:
    image: mongo:7.0
    environment:
      MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_USERNAME: 
      MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_PASSWORD: 
      MONGO_INITDB_DATABASE: 
    ports:
      - "27017:"
    volumes:
      - ./data/mongo:/data/db
  qdrant:
    image: qdrant/qdrant:v1.16.0  
    ports:
      - "6333:"
    volumes:
      - ./data/qdrant:/qdrant/storage

Q: How can I find the number of occurrences of a string in a file using the Windows command line? A:

It seems many respondents missed the original specification that all email addresses occur on one line. This means unless you introduce a CRLF with each occurrence of the @ symbol, your suggestions to use variants of FINDSTR /c will not help.

Among the Unix tools for DOS is the very powerful SED.exe. Google it. It rocks with regular expressions. Here's a suggestion:

find "@" datafile.txt | find "@" | sed "s/@/@\n/g" | find /n "@" | SED "s/\[\(.*\)\].*/Set \/a NumFound=\1/">CountChars.bat

Explanation (assuming the file with the data is named "Datafile.txt"):

  1. The first FIND includes three lines of header information, which throws of a line-count approach, so pipe the results to a second (identical) find to strip off unwanted header information.

  2. Pipe the above results to SED, which will search for each "@" character and replace it with itself+ "\n" (which is a "new line" AKA a CRLF) which gets each "@" on its own line in the output stream...

  3. When you pipe the above output from SED into the FIND /n command, you'll be adding line numbers to the beginning of each line. Now, all you have to do is isolate the numeric portion of each line and preface it with "SET /a" to convert each line into a batch statement that (increasingly with each line) sets the variable equal to that line's number.

  4. isolate each line's numeric part and preface the isolated number per the above via:

| SED "s/\[\(.*\)\].*/Set \/a NumFound=\1/"

In the above snippet, you're piping the previous command's output to SED, which uses this syntax "s/WhatToLookFor/WhatToReplaceItWith/", to do these steps:

a) look for a "[" (which must be "escaped" by prefacing it with "")

b) begin saving (or "tokenizing") what follows, up to the closing "]"

```lang-none
--> in other words it ignores the brackets but stores the number
--> the ".*" that follows the bracket wildcards whatever follows the "]"
```

c) the stuff between the \( and the \) is "tokenized", which means it can be referred-to later, in the "WhatToReplaceItWith" section. The first stuff that's tokenized is referred to via "\1" then second as "\2", etc.

So... we're ignoring the [ and the ] and we're saving the number that lies between the brackets and IGNORING all the wild-carded remainder of each line... thus we're replacing the line with the literal string:

`Set /a NumFound=`  + the saved, or "tokenized" number, i.e.
   ...the first line will read:  `Set /a NumFound=1`
   ...& the next line reads:     `Set /a NumFound=2`   etc. etc.

Thus, if you have 1,283 email addresses, your results will have 1,283 lines.

The last one executed = the one that matters.

If you use the ">" character to redirect all of the above output to a batch file, i.e.:

`> CountChars.bat`

...then just call that batch file, and you'll have a DOS environment variable named "NumFound" with your answer.

Q: How to save a screenshot of the contents of an FMX component without seeing only black image? A:

A TLayout has no content initially, especially not a background. When placed on a form, it will show whatever is on the form behind it. When you call MyFMXLayout.MakeScreenshot the color of the form, or any drawing element behind the TLayout will not be considered, as they would not be part of the TLayout. Instead, an area without any drawing elements is considered black (because a null color of a bitmap is displayed as black).

Now, if you draw your lines and figures with a black pen, they will not be visible against the black background.

Therefore, You must either fill the background with a color, e.g. white, before you draw your shapes in black. You can do that by adding a filled rectangle before any drawing.

Alternatively you can leave the background black and draw your shapes with a white (or other light) color.

Q: Is there any difference between a GUID and a UUID? A:

That depends on what GUID refers to. The Microsoft GUID is not compliant with the RFC 9562 UUID and has multiple differences.

When I am using the term Microsoft GUID, I refer to the kind of GUID as used in COM, OLE, or the Compound File Binary Format (CFBF).

Difference 1: The Windows GUID has a different byte layout than the RFC 9562 UUID.

The table below shows how GUID 00112233-4455-6677-8899-AABBCCDDEEFF is serialized as an RFC 9562 UUID versus a Windows GUID:

UUID / GUID type Serialized byte layout (hexadecimal)
RFC 9562 UUID layout 00 11 22 33 44 55 66 77 88 99 AA BB CC DD EE FF
Windows GUID layout 33 22 11 00 55 44 77 66 88 99 AA BB CC DD EE FF

Per field (the portion between dashes), the byte order differs for some fields:

Field (RFC 9562 description) UUID Windows GUID
4hexOctet "-" network byte order little endian
2hexOctet "-" network byte order little endian
2hexOctet "-" network byte order little endian
2hexOctet "-" network byte order network byte order
6hexOctet network byte order network byte order

Where the RFC 9562 UUID uses network byte order consistently, the Microsoft GUID uses mixed endianness.

Difference 2: Windows GUIDs do not require RFC 9562 variant and version semantics

Windows GUIDs are treated as opaque 128-bit values. Unlike RFC 9562 UUIDs, Windows does not require the variant or version bits to be set to meaningful values.

For example, the "NULL GUID": 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000:

  • Version field: In an RFC 9562 UUID, bits 12–15 of the time_hi_and_version field must encode a version from 1–8. In this GUID, those bits are 0000, which is version 0, an undefined value in the RFC.

  • Variant field: The variant bits are also 0b000, which does not correspond to any RFC-defined variant.

Another example is (documented here):

0002E005-0000-0000-C000-000000000046

This GUID identifies the Standard Component Categories Manager, a real COM class implemented by Windows. It uses an undefined version value and the Microsoft-reserved variant, making it invalid as an RFC 9562 UUID while remaining a perfectly valid Windows GUID.
